correctness.rationale: Ringel's orientable genus formula gives ceil(2*7/4)=4. A connected cellular embedding then has 17 faces and 72 total face sides. Bipartiteness forces even facial walk lengths; a length-two walk in this simple graph would immediately reverse the sole edge between its vertices, impossible under rotations at vertices of degrees 4 and 9. Thus the excess over 17 quadrangles is 4, split as 2+2 or 4. Both printed rotations were independently parsed and checked against the snapshot's witness data, then traced as permutations of all 72 darts. Each yielded 17 cycles and Euler characteristic -6. A gave 15 quadrangles and the two cyclic words (0,11,2,8,1,7), (1,12,2,9,3,11); B gave 16 quadrangles and the octagon (0,10,1,7,2,9,3,5). The rotation-system construction gives orientable cellular embeddings; there is no assumption that facial walks of arbitrary competing embeddings are simple cycles. Replay: python3 /workspace/replay/02-trace.py. The snapshot retains witness data, but its old verifier hardcodes scratch/witnesses.json and was not executed or treated as fresh verification.

evidence: For (4,9), h=4g-(m-2)(n-2)=2, so the prior excess theorem mechanically implies the exclusion half.

For (4,10), g=4 and excess zero. In a genus-4 cellular embedding all faces are quadrangles; a length-four walk cannot repeat a vertex without immediate reversal in this simple bipartite graph of minimum degree four. A degree-four vertex in the larger part is therefore incident to four distinct face walks. Deleting its four darts and their reverses from the rotation system splices the four face walks in cyclic order to one walk of length 4(4-2)=8, leaving all other face walks unchanged. This yields the octagonal profile on K(4,9), irrespective of the symmetry in SCOPE063.

Specializing the broader October 25 catalog finding at n=9 gives fifteen quadrangles and two hexagons. Its prior-work paragraph identifies the older finite census only through K(4,7) and does not ascribe a uniform extension to it.

value.rationale: The complete-bipartite minimum-genus face census is an established problem. K(4,9) is the first n>7 in the fixed K(4,n) family with nonzero orientable minimum-genus excess, naturally just beyond the cited small-part census. The substantive witness realizes two hexagons and establishes that the excess can be spent in a different way from the octagon obtained by deleting a vertex of K(4,10). It closes the exact finite census question at that boundary; the Euler calculation or the deletion construction alone would not suffice.
